scope_summary: Prime coat application for bare drywall wall surfaces in new construction. Single prime coat (no finish coats). Assumes drywall is taped, mudded, and sanded by drywall contractor prior to painting scope.
relevant_findings: PVA (polyvinyl acetate) primer is the standard choice for new drywall - economical, seals porous surface, excellent for latex topcoats
Acrylic latex primers offer superior adhesion and stain blocking for premium work (QT4)
High-build primers may be required for Level 5 drywall finish to achieve uniform porosity
New construction drywall typically has 'Good' surface condition with minimal defects
Spray+backroll is the most common production method in NC for speed and quality balance
Single primer coat is standard - drywall absorbs primer uniformly when properly prepared
Spot-priming fasteners is critical to prevent rust bleed-through on finish coats
Drywall dust is the primary contamination concern - must be removed before priming

prep_requirements.reason: Drywall dust reduces adhesion and causes visible contamination in primer film

prep_requirements.method: Walk with work light, mark defects
prep_requirements.reason: Identify fastener pops, unfilled joints, damaged paper before priming
prep_requirements.skip_conditions: QT2 may reduce to major defects only

prep_requirements.reason: Prevent rust bleed-through on finish coats
prep_requirements.skip_conditions: Never - always required for quality work

drywall_finish_level_impacts.description: Tape embedded in joint compound, two coats on joints and one on fasteners
drywall_finish_level_impacts.impact_on_prime: Higher absorption, may show joint pattern through single prime coat
drywall_finish_level_impacts.notes: Acceptable for utility areas, may need second prime for visible areas

drywall_finish_level_impacts.description: Level 3 plus additional skim coat on joints and fasteners
drywall_finish_level_impacts.impact_on_prime: Standard absorption, single prime coat typically sufficient
drywall_finish_level_impacts.notes: Most common in residential and commercial NC

drywall_finish_level_impacts.impact_on_prime: Uniform surface, good primer holdout, may require light sand after prime
drywall_finish_level_impacts.notes: Required for high sheen finishes, critical lighting conditions

common_failure_modes.cause: Fasteners not spot-primed, rust migrates through topcoat
common_failure_modes.prevention: Always spot-prime fastener locations before full coat
common_failure_modes.remediation: Sand affected area, apply shellac-based primer, reprime

common_failure_modes.cause: Different absorption rates between joint compound and paper face
common_failure_modes.prevention: Use high-build primer for Level 3 drywall, consider double prime
common_failure_modes.remediation: Additional primer coat, consider high-build product

common_failure_modes.cause: Drywall dust contamination, primer applied too thick
Insufficient inspection, poor technique with spray
common_failure_modes.prevention: Work with adequate lighting, overlap passes

common_failure_modes.cause: Inconsistent mil thickness, lap marks from slow technique
common_failure_modes.prevention: Maintain wet edge, consistent application speed
common_failure_modes.remediation: Light sand and reprime if severe

required_paintscope_keys.description: Total paintable wall field area (excluding openings)
required_paintscope_keys.required_when: Always - primary quantity driver for wall priming

required_paintscope_keys.description: Linear footage of wall-to-ceiling boundary for edge cut-in
required_paintscope_keys.required_when: When quality_tier is QT3 or QT4 (edge work priced separately)

adjacency_notes.scope_impact: May require brush cut-in if ceiling is separate phase or different product
adjacency_notes.nc_context: In NC, ceilings are typically primed before walls. Wall primer should extend to ceiling line but not onto ceiling.

adjacency_notes.scope_impact: Typically NOT included in wall prime scope - trim is sprayed separately
adjacency_notes.nc_context: In NC production, trim is primed/painted after walls, so wall prime stops at trim line without edge detail

adjacency_notes.scope_impact: Inside corners - no special treatment needed for priming
adjacency_notes.nc_context: Corners are rolled/sprayed continuously, no separate edge work

notes_for_materials_manager: PVA primer is default for QT2-QT3, acrylic latex for QT4
Coverage rates: ~350 SF/gal smooth, ~275 SF/gal textured, ~200 SF/gal high-build
Primer selection should match topcoat manufacturer when possible
VOC compliance required in some jurisdictions - verify local requirements
notes_for_sop_librarian: Vacuum step is CRITICAL - drywall dust causes adhesion failure
Spot-prime fasteners regardless of QT to prevent bleed-through
Spray+backroll modules need coupling constraint (backroll sets pace)
Edge cut-in timing differs: roll method = cut first; spray method = touch-up after
QT4 may add light sand after prime for Level 5 finish
notes_for_estimation_engineer: Roll rates: ~350 SF/hr smooth, ~275 SF/hr textured
Spray rates: ~600-700 SF/hr but limited by backroll if using spray+backroll
Edge cut-in: ~100 LF/hr standard, ~75 LF/hr for crisp QT4 edges
Effective spray+backroll rate is backroll rate (coupling constraint)
assumptions: All drywall is standard gypsum board (not specialized types like moisture-resistant or fire-rated)
New construction surface condition is 'Good' - minimal defects expected
Standard ceiling heights 8-10 ft (adjust rates for higher ceilings)
Drywall contractor has completed all taping, mudding, and sanding
No remediation of drywall damage in scope (painter responsible for prime only)
Adequate ventilation available for primer dry time
uncertainties: Drywall finish quality varies by contractor - may need field adjustment to prep scope
Whether fastener spot-priming should be separate line item or included in prep assumption
Impact of humidity on dry times and recoat windows
Spray tip selection for different primer viscosities
